questions.text: Cast-in-place (CIP) concrete construction involves pouring concrete on-site with temporary formwork support. What are the primary components of the CIP process?

options.text: Formwork, rebar placement, concrete pouring, vibration, and curing in place
Precast elements delivered and bolted together, which eliminates the need for on-site concrete pouring and formwork
Formwork design only; concrete is delivered pre-mixed and does not require on-site adjustments or additional mixing
Rebar installation without concrete placement, focusing solely on the structural reinforcement aspect

rationale.b: Precast involves factory fabrication and on-site assembly, not in-place construction.
rationale.c: CIP requires active curing processes, not passive delivery.
rationale.d: Concrete placement and curing are integral to CIP.
rationale.correct: CIP construction consists of building temporary formwork, placing reinforcement per drawings, pouring concrete (by pump or bucket), vibrating to consolidate, and curing moisture/temperature-controlled on-site. All strength gain occurs in place, enabling site customization and monolithic structural behavior.

questions.text: Concrete reinforcement is placed with cover (distance from concrete surface to rebar) of typically ___ mm for beams and columns, and ___ mm for slabs. Why is adequate cover essential?

options.text: 40 mm for beams/columns, 20 mm for slabs. Cover protects rebar from carbonation (acid attack) and chloride corrosion in wet/coastal environments.
10 mm for all members; thickness is immaterial, as modern concrete additives provide sufficient protection
100 mm minimum; thicker cover is always safer, ensuring maximum durability against environmental factors
Cover is only required for exposed elements; internal members need none, as they are naturally protected by surrounding concrete

rationale.b: Minimal cover (10 mm) provides little protection; corrosion reaches rebar within years.
rationale.c: Excessive cover (100 mm) increases section size, weight, and cost without proportional durability gain.
rationale.d: Internal members are still exposed to moisture and humidity; cover is universal.
rationale.correct: NSCP 2015 Table 412-4.1 specifies minimum cover: 40 mm for beams and columns, 20 mm for slabs (interior and exterior). Cover depth protects embedded steel from carbonation (CO₂ diffusion) and chloride penetration (salt spray in coastal areas). Insufficient cover leads to early corrosion, rust expansion, spalling, and loss of load-bearing capacity.

questions.text: Concrete is over-vibrated during placement. What are the likely consequences?

options.text: Segregation (coarse aggregate settling), surface blowholes, and reduced strength in upper layers due to excessive air removal and paste separation.
Improved consolidation; over-vibration always benefits concrete quality, leading to a denser and more uniform material
No effect; vibration duration is irrelevant, as concrete properties are unaffected by over-vibration
Enhanced bond with rebar; over-vibration is desirable, ensuring better structural integrity

rationale.b: Over-vibration degrades quality, not improves it.
rationale.c: Vibration duration has major impact on quality.
rationale.d: Over-vibration reduces bond by causing paste separation.
rationale.correct: Over-vibration causes segregation: coarse aggregate settles while paste rises, creating weak upper layers and voids below. Surface blowholes (small bubble cavities) indicate excess air removal and paste migration. Under-vibration leaves voids and poor consolidation. Proper vibration (20–30 seconds per placement zone) is optimum; operator training and equipment maintenance are critical for quality.

questions.text: A precast hollow-core slab system is compared to cast-in-place concrete for a 20-story apartment building. Which statement accurately captures the trade-off?

options.text: Precast: faster on-site assembly, reduced on-site formwork, but requires factory production time and transportation logistics. CIP: longer on-site construction but enables site customization and no transportation constraints. For 20 stories, precast is likely faster if production and logistics are planned efficiently.
Precast is always faster regardless of project scale, which may not account for specific logistical challenges
CIP is always more economical; precast has no cost advantage, which oversimplifies the cost analysis
Precast and CIP have identical construction schedules, which is rarely the case in practice

rationale.b: Precast has advantages but requires logistics planning; not universally faster for all projects.
rationale.c: Precast often has cost advantages in high-rise due to reduced labor.
rationale.d: Schedules differ significantly; precast faster on-site.
rationale.correct: Precast excels for repetitive elements in mid-to-high-rise buildings. Factory production and on-site assembly occur in parallel, reducing critical path. CIP requires sequential on-site formwork, curing, and removal. However, precast's factory production time, transportation, and careful installation logistics must be managed. For 20 stories with repetitive floor plans, precast is typically faster if planned effectively.

questions.text: Precast concrete hollow-core slabs offer advantages over cast-in-place slabs including lighter self-weight and reduced on-site formwork. Typical span range for hollow-core units is ___–___ meters.

options.text: 6–12 meters
1–3 meters
15–30 meters
30+ meters

rationale.b: 1–3 m is too short for efficient precast economics; CIP is competitive.
rationale.c: 15–30 m is the Double-Tee range, not hollow-core.
rationale.d: 30+ m requires specialized systems beyond standard precast.
rationale.correct: Hollow-core slabs are economical for spans of 6–12 m. The internal void cores reduce weight while maintaining stiffness. Double-Tee (DT) beams cover longer spans (12–30 m). Very long spans (30+ m) typically use cable-stayed or suspension systems.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Chapter 4; PCI Precast Design Manual

questions.text: Precast connections are either wet (grouted) or dry (bolted/welded). A moment-resisting frame requires structural continuity to redistribute seismic forces. Which connection type is more appropriate and why?

options.text: Wet (grouted) connections provide structural continuity similar to monolithic CIP behavior and allow moment transfer between precast elements. However, they require 7–14 day grout curing before load application.
Dry (bolted) connections are always superior for moment-resisting frames, especially in seismic zones where flexibility is prioritized over rigidity.
Wet and dry connections offer identical moment-transfer capacity, making them interchangeable in all structural applications without any impact on performance.
Precast elements cannot be used in moment-resisting frames; only CIP is suitable due to its inherent ability to handle dynamic loads without additional reinforcement.

rationale.b: Dry connections can transfer moments via carefully designed bolted plates, but wet is simpler and more reliable.
rationale.c: Wet and dry have different structural behavior; wet is preferred for moment transfer.
rationale.d: Modern precast systems effectively resist seismic loads with proper connections.
rationale.correct: Wet (grouted) connections fill voids with cementitious grout, locking precast units together and enabling moment transfer similar to CIP. They are preferred for moment-resisting frames. Dry (bolted) connections are mechanical and simpler to install but require careful design to transfer moments via bolted plate connections. Grout curing delay (7–14 days) must be accommodated in schedules; dry connections permit immediate load application.

questions.text: A concrete beam in a Philippine coastal building is designed with rebar cover of 30 mm instead of the specified 40 mm due to construction error. The beam is exposed to marine salt spray. What is the long-term durability risk?

options.text: Carbonation and chloride penetration will reach the rebar within 5–10 years (vs. 20+ years with adequate 40 mm cover). Rust expansion causes spalling, cracking, and loss of structural capacity. Repair/replacement is necessary before design service life (50 years) is achieved.
30 mm cover is adequate; marine salt spray does not penetrate concrete, assuming the concrete mix has a water-cement ratio below 0.40 and is properly cured.
Durability risk is minimal if concrete strength is high, provided that the concrete has been treated with a surface sealant to prevent chloride ingress.
Cover thickness is cosmetic; structural capacity is unaffected unless the beam is subjected to direct impact or heavy loading conditions.

rationale.b: Salt spray is highly aggressive; even good concrete cannot prevent chloride penetration over decades.
rationale.c: High concrete strength slows but does not prevent chloride penetration; cover is the primary defense.
rationale.d: Cover is structural; it directly impacts service life and durability.
rationale.correct: NSCP 2015 Section 402 (Durability) specifies cover based on exposure. For coastal (marine salt spray) environments, 50 mm cover is required to protect rebar for 50 years. Reducing cover to 30 mm accelerates corrosion—chloride ions from salt spray penetrate concrete and reach rebar within 5–10 years, initiating rust. Rust expansion (volume increase of ~5%) causes concrete spalling, water ingress, and further deterioration. Early major repairs are likely, failing the 50-year design intent.

questions.text: A 25-story residential tower in Manila will use precast hollow-core floor slabs with wet (grouted) connections to support structures. The developer requests design verification that the project can be completed in 24 months including 6 months of design/permitting. Evaluate feasibility considering production time, transportation, on-site assembly, and grouted connection curing.

options.text: Feasible if carefully planned: Precast production can occur during construction of lower levels (parallel path). On-site assembly is rapid (~1 day per floor). However, 7–14 day grout curing between floors delays load transfer. Critical path is 6 mo. design + 3–4 mo. production + 3–4 mo. assembly/curing + contingency = ~18 months construction. Margin exists for 24-month total if production and logistics are managed efficiently. Risks: production delays, transportation bottlenecks, weather-induced curing delays in rainy season.
Impossible; precast projects always exceed 36 months, which is a common misconception
Feasible with no schedule risk or contingency needed, which is overly optimistic given typical project challenges
Grout curing delay is immaterial; assembly can continue without waiting, which ignores structural integrity concerns

rationale.b: Precast schedules vary greatly by planning; 24 months is achievable with diligence.
rationale.c: Tight schedules always involve risk; contingency is necessary.
rationale.d: Grout curing delays can extend overall schedule if not managed; assembly cannot safely load until grout sets.
rationale.correct: Timeline analysis: design/permits 6 mo., precast production 3–4 mo. (parallel to foundation/lower structure), on-site assembly ~3–4 mo. (1 day/floor + grout curing delays), finishing 2–3 mo. Total: ~18 months construction fits within 24 months (assuming 6 mo. design). Grout curing (7–14 days between floors where loads transfer) is the main schedule risk. If planned as sequential phases (grout cures while assembly continues on levels above), critical path is manageable. Tropical rainy season (June–October) may reduce curing speed; schedule accordingly.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Chapter 4; PCI Project Planning Guide

questions.text: ACI 347 specifies that formwork for horizontal spans should not be struck until concrete achieves approximately ___ percent of the design 28-day strength. Why is this timing critical in Philippine tropical climates?

options.text: 70%; Inadequate early strength risks sagging, cracking, and water ingress. Tropical high humidity and potential rain exposure during curing demand conservative strength targets before load application.
50%; Lower strength is acceptable since tropical warmth accelerates curing, reducing the time needed for formwork removal
90%; Maximum curing delay, but necessary for durability, especially in environments with fluctuating temperatures and humidity
25%; Rapid form removal to accelerate schedule, although this may compromise structural integrity if not carefully managed

rationale.b: 50% is too low; bending capacity is insufficient.
rationale.c: 90% is overly conservative; strength gain plateaus after 28 days.
rationale.d: 25% is dangerously low; failure is likely.
rationale.correct: ACI 347 recommends 70% of 28-day strength before striking forms. In Philippine tropical climates with variable humidity, monsoon rain, and warm temperatures, early strength gain may be unpredictable. Conservative 70% threshold (achieved typically at 7–14 days for standard Portland cement) ensures safe form removal without risk of collapse or excessive deflection. Premature removal risks sagging, cracking, and water infiltration compromising durability.

questions.text: Conventional timber formwork (coco lumber) reuses approximately ___ cycles before replacement, whereas system formwork (aluminum/steel) achieves ___ cycles. Why is system formwork preferred for high-rise buildings despite higher capital cost?

options.text: Conventional: 5–10 cycles; System: 50+ cycles. System formwork reduces labor assembly time per floor and enables rapid form striking, accelerating high-rise construction schedules. The labor savings justify the capital investment.
Conventional: 50+; System: 5–10. Conventional is always superior, especially in terms of cost-effectiveness and ease of handling for smaller projects.
Both achieve identical cycles; cost is the only difference, although system formwork is often chosen for its perceived durability and ease of use in complex designs.
System formwork is heavier and unsuitable for heights above 20 stories, which limits its application in high-rise construction projects where weight is a critical factor.

rationale.b: Conventional reuses fewer times; system is designed for hundreds of uses.
rationale.c: System and conventional reverse the cycle counts.
rationale.d: System is not weight-limited; it's used up to 100+ stories globally.
rationale.correct: Conventional timber formwork (coco lumber) reuses ~5–10 times before degradation; system aluminum/steel panels achieve 50+ cycles. For high-rise projects with 30+ floors, system formwork's rapid assembly, standardized connections, and minimal adjustment time per floor reduce total labor cost despite higher capital outlay. Conventional timber is economical for low-rise (1–5 floors).
